clue.text: Blonde type picked for Wimbledon

blocks.note: first meaning: a ... blonde has reddish-gold hair
second meaning: the fruit gathered to be served with cream at the tennis championships

explanation.surface: A fair-haired player is selected for the Wimbledon tennis tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked' suggests a player chosen for a team, but it is fruit-picking: strawberries and cream are the traditional treat at Wimbledon, the London tennis championships.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit names a reddish shade of fair hair and is the famous snack eaten by spectators at the tennis.

clue.text: Used in garden when drier, about middle of March

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase, thing used in garden, standing for the noun

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, so only that one is kept
about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: a towel is something you dry yourself with
the central letter of the five-letter month

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a tool is used in the garden once the soil has dried, around mid-March.
explanation.walkthrough: TOWEL wraps round R to give TROWEL. 'Drier' looks like a comparison of weather but is a thing that dries.
explanation.definitionFit: A trowel is a small hand tool for digging, employed by gardeners when planting bulbs and seedlings.

clue.text: Suspension of a governor can trouble East

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so these letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
a bey was a governor of a province in the Ottoman Empire
taken as written, to be mixed
E is the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A regional governor is suspended because he could stir up trouble in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can trouble' reads as a verb phrase, could cause trouble, but 'can' is fodder and 'trouble' the instruction to shuffle it with E.
explanation.definitionFit: Abeyance is a state of temporary disuse or postponement, so a matter held in abeyance is suspended.

clue.text: Vital necessity to supply for best horses

blocks.note: blood is the fluid without which no body can live
to stock a shop is to supply it with goods

explanation.surface: Something essential must be provided for the finest racehorses.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloodstock is the trade term for thoroughbred horses bred for racing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloodstock means thoroughbreds collectively, the pedigree animals bred for racing and sold at premium sales.

clue.text: Arrange outfit round poles in putting washing out

indicators.note: round means encircling, so the first piece is wrapped about what follows

blocks.note: to rig out is to dress or equip someone
the north and south poles, N and S
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sorts clothes around the posts before hanging out the laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' suggests washing-line props, but they are the north and south poles; 'in' is taken literally and joins them inside the outfit word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rinsing is clearing soap or dirt from something with clean water, which is washing it out.

clue.text: Measure the main beam

blocks.note: first meaning: a length of three feet
second meaning: a spar hung from a ship's mast; the main is the sea

explanation.surface: Someone is told to measure the principal beam of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like principal, but it is the old word for the open sea, so the beam belongs on a sailing ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an imperial length unit and the horizontal spar that carries a ship's sail.

clue.text: Times read here to be better informed?

definitions.text: Times read here to be better informed?

blocks.note: surface: a place to read The Times newspaper; actually a list of race starting times
surface: more knowledgeable; actually a punter, one who bets, getting information

explanation.surface: A reading room where people consult The Times to become more knowledgeable.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T of 'Times' points at this very newspaper, but the times are the starting times of races, and 'better' is someone placing bets.
explanation.definitionFit: A racecard is the printed programme at a race meeting listing runners, riders and starting times for punters.

clue.text: Precocious literary effort is very easy

blocks.note: first meaning: a drama written by a youngster
second meaning: a task needing no effort at all

explanation.surface: A gifted youngster's writing turns out to be no trouble at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a task so simple even a youngster could do it, and literally names a drama by a young author.

clue.text: A jolly peculiar hag, but county

indicators.note: peculiar means odd, so these letters appear in an odd order

blocks.note: taken as written
a jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An old woman is described as very odd, yet thoroughly provincial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly peculiar' reads as 'very strange', but 'jolly' is a Royal Marine and only 'peculiar' acts on the hag.
explanation.definitionFit: Armagh is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, so it is an example of a county.

clue.text: Poet and saint named old card game

blocks.note: Alexander Pope, the eighteenth-century English poet
Saint Joan, Joan of Arc

explanation.surface: A writer and a holy figure lend their names to a game of cards from long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope Joan was also a legendary female pope, which gives the game its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope Joan is a Victorian-era card game played with a special staking board, now rarely seen.

clue.text: Concerning stars of team — Madrid one

blocks.note: a side is a sports team
Real Madrid, the Spanish football club

explanation.surface: A piece about the star players of a team, namely Real Madrid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars of team' sounds like celebrated footballers, but the definition is astronomical and 'team' is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidereal means relating to the fixed stars, as in a sidereal day measured against them.

clue.text: A tribe, in poetic language

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the phrase that follows

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and the first three of the second

explanation.surface: A tribal community described in the flowery words of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A clan is a group of families claiming common descent, the Scottish counterpart of a tribe.

clue.text: Force prison, perhaps, to have restraints

indicators.note: perhaps says the word is only one possible ordering of its letters

blocks.note: to cram is to force or stuff something in
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Inmates are forced into jail so that they can be held in restraints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prison, perhaps' looks like an example of a place of restraint, yet 'perhaps' is telling you to shuffle the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cramp-irons are iron bars with bent ends used to clamp stones or timbers together, holding them as restraints.

clue.text: Present manager, alas, can't reform us

indicators.note: to reform is to form again in a new shape, so the letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter, ignoring the comma and apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: A frustrated employee laments that the current boss cannot change our ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as current, as in the manager now in charge, but it is a noun: the gifts.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure who organises and delivers Christmas gifts is jokingly called the one who manages presents.

clue.text: Charged with holding up MOT as usual

indicators.note: holding means keeping inside, so the first word wraps what follows
in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: charged with a crime is accused
the vehicle test, taken as written

explanation.surface: A motorist is charged for keeping an MOT certificate, as normally happens.
explanation.walkthrough: An MOT is the UK's annual roadworthiness test for cars; 'holding up' looks like delaying it, but splits into a container and a reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Accustomed, in the sense of customary or habitual, describes what is usual, as in his accustomed seat.

clue.text: Undercurrent?

blocks.note: surface: a hidden flow beneath the surface of water or a hidden feeling
setter's reading: a current, that is a river, flowing in the underworld

explanation.walkthrough: Split it as under-current: in Greek myth this river of the underworld was crossed by the dead in Charon's boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Acheron is the mythological river of woe in Hades, a flowing stream located beneath the earth.

clue.text: Bill's place for storing up food, for example

blocks.note: first meaning: a billboard where posters, or bills, are pasted
second meaning: amassing supplies and keeping them hidden

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill has a larder where food is stockpiled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is a poster.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a large board for advertising posters and the act of stockpiling goods.

clue.text: One in Bohemia involved the woman

definitions.text: One in Bohemia involved the woman

blocks.clueFragment: One in Bohemia involved the woman
blocks.note: surface: an affair in central Europe with some lady
setter's reading: the italic phrase is Sherlock Holmes's name for Irene Adler, heroine of a Conan Doyle story set in Bohemia

explanation.surface: A Bohemian man had an affair with a certain woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics flag a quotation: Holmes always called Irene Adler 'the woman', and her story is titled A ___ in Bohemia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Conan Doyle story concerns a disgraceful affair threatening a king, which is exactly a public outrage.

clue.text: One becoming active, now light is bad

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters have gone wrong and need putting into a different order

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone stirs into action now that the daylight is poor.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition needs the surface context: the person comes alive just as the light fails.
explanation.definitionFit: A late-hours person is lively after dark, waking up when others go to bed, like the nocturnal bird.

clue.text: Place for fuel — in sink?

blocks.note: first meaning: a coal container by the fireplace
second meaning: to sink a ship deliberately by holing it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the kitchen sink is the spot to keep fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like the kitchen basin, but it is a verb about ships.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal scuttle is a bucket for fuel, and to scuttle a vessel is to send it to the bottom.

clue.text: Conversions, perhaps, bring job satisfaction of exciting kind

blocks.note: a place is a position of employment
getting your kicks is getting thrills

explanation.surface: Religious conversions might give a thrilling sense of fulfilment at work.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby a conversion is the kick at goal after a try, taken with the ball resting on the ground; 'perhaps' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A rugby conversion is taken as a kick from a ball set on the ground, so conversions are examples.

clue.text: Pass the fish!

blocks.note: first meaning: to move past, as time does
second meaning: a small spiny-finned sea creature

explanation.surface: A diner asks for the fish dish to be handed across the table.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads as a table request, but 'Pass' is a verb meaning elapse and the fish is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to move past or elapse, and the single word names a small coastal fish.

clue.text: “And the soul wears out the —” (Byron)

blocks.clueFragment: And the soul wears out the
blocks.note: a line from Byron's poem So We'll Go No More a Roving
the poet's name tells the solver to complete his line from memory

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: Byron wrote 'For the sword outwears its sheath, / And the soul wears out the breast', and the missing word completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The chest is the part of the body that houses the heart and, poetically, the soul, so it wears out.

clue.text: Great Russian space traveller?

blocks.note: Red was the common label for a Soviet Russian
giant means very great in size

explanation.surface: A celebrated Soviet cosmonaut is hailed as a great Russian in space.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a cosmonaut; the question mark admits that calling a star a traveller in space is a stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A red giant is a large ageing star, a body moving through the heavens, playfully called a traveller.

clue.text: Assist offender as a matter of course

blocks.note: taken as written
a wager is the business of the racecourse

explanation.surface: Helping a criminal is described as something routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a matter of course' reads as an idiom meaning routinely; split it and the course is a racecourse, where a bet is the matter in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to help or encourage someone in wrongdoing, a legal term in aiding and abetting.

clue.text: Sometime employee said to be worldly

blocks.note: a temp is a worker employed only now and then
spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: A former employee is reported to be sophisticated and experienced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sometime' usually means former, but here it means occasional, the way a temporary worker is.
explanation.definitionFit: Temporal means of this world and its time, secular, as opposed to spiritual or eternal matters.

clue.text: Minority position of one eccentric about horse

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters go out of order
about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: Someone describes the awkward standing of an odd person regarding horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minority' suggests a smaller group, but here it is the legal term for being under age.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonage is the legal state of being under age, which lawyers call minority, a position held until adulthood.

clue.text: Instrument used to survey the limestone round front of Downs

indicators.note: round means encircling, so the rock word goes about the next letter
the front of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: taken as written
oolite is a limestone made of tiny rounded grains
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Surveyors map limestone around the chalk hills of the South Downs with a measuring device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to survey the limestone' looks like one phrase; the definition stops at 'survey'. Oolite is a geologist's word worth knowing for crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A theodolite is a surveyor's optical instrument on a tripod for measuring horizontal and vertical angles.
